rv.q: “The Monsters” is an insistence on the softness living in even our hardest men; it’s a tenderness the world tries to extinguish that must be wrestled back.
Writer-director Ngozi Anyanwu stages these sequences with thrilling immediacy, aided by choreographer Rickey Tripp and fight director Gerry Rodriguez.
The Monsters is a rare fusion of muscular physicality and emotional depth, a production that hits hard in every sense and earns every one of its bruises.
The New Jersey-born of Nigerian parentage Anyanwu in The Monsters demonstrates a supreme command of dramatic writing.
You will not soon forget Aigner Mizzelle’s Lil or Okieriete Onaodowan’s Big or their struggle to overcome their abusive childhood.

Okieriete ‘Oak’ Onaodowan and Aigner Mizzelle are every bit as adept in the emotional dance between their characters as they are in the physical interaction enacted on stage with the aid of a choreographer, a fight director, and an “MMA consultant.”

Ms. Anyanwu originally subtitled “The Monsters” “a sibling love story,” and that’s pretty much a perfect summation of this simple but endearing play, which reminds us that while all kinds of love can be complicated, it’s important to roll with the punches.
The theatricality and performances on view in The Monsters offer a vital reminder that theatre can offer the same visceral experience as a high-stakes slugfest.
The cathartic outcome is satisfying – a good night in the ring with two alpha sibs!
The Monsters succeeds in its slow and steady gain of momentum as Big and Lil both work toward their next matches and try to repair their relationship.
But if you take away the cursing and the physical and mental sparring, this play never lands a solid punch.
The Monsters is a layered, emotionally muscular play powered by two formidable performances and technical flair that matches a script full of duels and drama alike.
The play is a gripping, deeply felt exploration of estranged siblings as they attempt to navigate their way back to one another.
This is Lil and Big’s story—a story of trying to overcome a past that also had Edenic elements that can never be fully regained—brought to poignant life in two superb performances.
The Monsters delivers a bruising, brilliant exploration of sibling trauma that lands nearly every emotional punch.
A tough, finely observed drama that hits with both muscle and heart.
These little movements and and the starts and ends of conversations are what keeps us focused, laughing, and believeing in the rebirth of siblings, together and apart.
The rest of the show, in contrast, was gray.

cn.t: Critics praise this emotionally bruising two-hander about estranged MMA fighter siblings, lauding Anyanwu's direction and the leads' performances. The intimate drama uses fighting as a metaphor for reconciliation, earning strong reviews for its emotional depth.

vr.q: this is overall a really strong and emotionally resonant piece
The emotional payoff speaks for itself... I ended up quite enjoying this.
